Une émotion prépare à agir: An emotion prepares you to act
Une émotion prépare une action (peur → f: An emotion prepares an action (fear → flee). Six basic emotions according to Ekman, universality debated.
Une émotion n'est pas un simple ressenti: An emotion is not just a feeling: it is the body getting ready to act. Faced with danger, the amygdala triggers a fast reaction, adrenaline speeds up the heart and readies the muscles: that is the "fight or flight" response. Fear is for fleeing, anger for defending yourself, disgust for rejecting what might poison you.
Dans les années 1960, Paul Ekman montre: In the 1960s Paul Ekman showed photos of faces to the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, who had little exposure to Western media: they recognised most of the expressions. He drew from this six basic emotions, joy, sadness, fear, anger, disgust and surprise. This universality is debated today: reading a face also depends on context and culture.
Nommer son émotion la calme (Lieberman,: Naming your emotion calms it (Lieberman, 2007). Reappraising works better than suppressing.
Mettre un mot sur ce qu'on ressent, « je: Putting a word on what you feel, "I feel anxious", already helps calm it: in 2007 Matthew Lieberman's team observed with brain imaging a drop in amygdala activity when an emotion is named. That is affect labelling.
Autre stratégie efficace : la réévaluati: Another effective strategy is reappraisal, which changes how you see the situation. Seeing stage fright as excitement rather than fear, for example. Conversely, systematically suppressing your emotions costs energy and does not reduce what you feel. The emotion is not the enemy; what matters is what you do with it.
Empathie émotionnelle (ressentir) et cog: Emotional empathy (feeling) and cognitive empathy (understanding). Active listening: restate to check.
L'empathie a deux faces. L'empathie émot: Empathy has two sides. Emotional empathy is feeling with the other person; cognitive empathy is understanding what they think or feel, without necessarily feeling it yourself. Emotions also spread without our thinking about it: that is emotional contagion, like a yawn or a fit of giggles.
Une compétence s'entraîne : l'écoute act: It is a skill you can train: active listening. Restating what the other person said, "if I understand correctly, you…", shows you have understood and lets them correct you. Daniel Goleman popularised the idea of "emotional intelligence" in 1995, a concept proposed by Peter Salovey and John Mayer in 1990.
Oubli rapide au début puis lent (Ebbingh: Fast forgetting at first, then slow (Ebbinghaus, 1885). Spaced reminders: far more effective than cramming.
Hermann Ebbinghaus fut son propre cobaye: Hermann Ebbinghaus was his own guinea pig. He learned lists of meaningless syllables, like "DAX" or "BOK", so that nothing would latch onto an existing memory, then measured what remained. In 1885 he published Über das Gedächtnis: we forget very fast at first, especially in the first hours, then more and more slowly.
Il découvre aussi l'effet d'espacement :: He also discovered the spacing effect: reviewing at spaced intervals retains far better than cramming everything at once. It is one of the most solid findings in the psychology of learning, and it is exactly what this game's reminders do. Each successful recall flattens the curve and lets you wait longer before the next one.
Mémoire de travail ≈ 7 ± 2 éléments (Mil: Working memory ≈ 7 ± 2 items (Miller, 1956). The hippocampus forms event memories (patient H. M.).
La mémoire de travail ne garde que quelq: Working memory holds only a few items, for a few seconds: George Miller, in 1956, spoke of about seven items, plus or minus two. Hence the point of grouping a phone number into pairs. Long-term memory is almost unlimited.
En 1953, pour soigner son épilepsie, on: In 1953, to treat his epilepsy, Henry Molaison had both hippocampi removed. He could no longer form new memories of events, but still learned new motor skills, without remembering having learned them. Patient H. M. showed that memory is not one thing: memory for facts goes through the hippocampus, memory for skills through other circuits. And sleep helps: the day's memories are replayed and stabilised then.
Se tester + espacer. Palais de mémoire :: Test yourself + space it out. Memory palace: place items in familiar places. We remember the start and end of a list best.
Relire et surligner donnent une impressi: Rereading and highlighting give a feeling of mastery: everything seems familiar. Testing yourself is far more effective: fetching information from memory strengthens it. Combined with spacing, it is the winning pair.
Pour le plaisir ou pour la récompense: For the pleasure or for the reward
Autonomie, compétence, lien social (Deci: Autonomy, competence, social connection (Deci and Ryan). Rewarding what you enjoy can kill the desire. Flow: difficulty that matches.
Edward Deci et Richard Ryan résument ce: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan sum up what feeds lasting motivation in three needs: autonomy, feeling you are behind your choices; competence, feeling you are progressing; and social connection. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi adds flow: we become absorbed in a task when its difficulty just matches our abilities. Too easy, we get bored; too hard, we get anxious.
La pyramide que Maslow n'a pas dessinée: The pyramid Maslow did not draw
Maslow n'a pas dessiné de pyramide (McDe: Maslow did not draw a pyramid (McDermid, 1960). The marshmallow test predicts far less than was thought (Watts, 2018).
Abraham Maslow propose en 1943 une hiéra: In 1943 Abraham Maslow proposed a hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualisation. But he never drew a pyramid. The famous shape comes from a business consultant psychologist, Charles McDermid, in 1960, and took hold in management textbooks.
Méfiance aussi envers le test du marshma: Be wary of the marshmallow test too. In the 1960s and 1970s Walter Mischel offered children one treat now or two if they waited; those who waited seemed to do better later. In 2018 a much larger replication by Tyler Watts and colleagues found a far weaker link, largely explained by family background. Waiting also makes more sense when you trust the adult making the promise.
Procrastiner = fuir une émotion. Commenc: Procrastinating = fleeing an emotion. Start for 5 minutes. A precise goal > "doing your best" (Locke and Latham).
Un objectif précis et mesurable motive d: A precise, measurable goal motivates more than "doing your best": that is a central finding of Edwin Locke and Gary Latham's theory. And to build a habit, a small regular action tied to a specific time of day beats a big, rare effort. Believing your abilities can develop, Carol Dweck's growth mindset, helps you persevere.
Face à un groupe unanime qui se trompe,: Faced with a unanimous group that is wrong, a third of answers go along (Asch, 1951). A single ally brings conformity down.
En 1951, Solomon Asch montre à des étudi: In 1951 Solomon Asch showed students a reference line and three lines to compare. The answer is obvious. But the participant is surrounded by accomplices who all give the same wrong answer out loud. About a third of answers follow the group, and 74 % of participants give in at least once.
Le résultat le plus encourageant est ail: The most encouraging finding lies elsewhere: it only takes one accomplice giving the right answer for conformity to collapse. With an ally, only 5 % keep following the majority. Daring to be the first to say no helps others say it too.
Milgram (1963) : 65 % vont jusqu'à 450 V: Milgram (1963): 65 % go up to 450 V under authority. Stanford (1971) is disputed; Genovese's "38 witnesses" are exaggerated.
En 1963, Stanley Milgram demande à des v: In 1963 Stanley Milgram asked volunteers to give increasingly strong electric shocks to a "learner" who made mistakes. The shocks were fake, the learner an actor who screamed. Under the calm pressure of an experimenter in a lab coat, 65 % of participants in the main version went up to the maximum 450-volt shock.
Toutes les expériences célèbres ne tienn: Not all famous experiments hold up as well. The Stanford prison experiment, run by Philip Zimbardo in 1971, is now heavily disputed: archives show the "guards" were encouraged to be harsh. And the story of Kitty Genovese, killed in 1964 in front of "38 witnesses" who did nothing, was exaggerated: there were far fewer, and the police were called.
Effet du témoin : plus on est nombreux,: Bystander effect: the more people, the less help (70 % alone against 40 % in pairs). Groupthink (Janis, 1972).
Quand plusieurs personnes assistent à un: When several people witness an emergency, each thinks someone else will act: responsibility is diluted. That is the bystander effect. In 1969 Bibb Latané and Judith Rodin had people hear a woman fall in the next room: 70 % of those alone went to help, against 40 % when paired with a stranger.
En groupe, les opinions se durcissent au: In groups, opinions also harden: group polarisation pushes towards the already dominant position. And groupthink can lead experts to bad collective decisions: Irving Janis illustrated it in 1972 with the failed Bay of Pigs landing. Antidote: appoint a devil's advocate, and ask for opinions before the leader gives theirs.
≈ 86 milliards de neurones (Herculano-Ho: ≈ 86 billion neurons (Herculano-Houzel, 2009), ≈ 20 W. Distinct neurons (Cajal, Nobel 1906). The 10 % myth is false.
Le cerveau compte environ 86 milliards d: The brain has about 86 billion neurons, according to Suzana Herculano-Houzel's count in 2009; the often-quoted 100 billion had never been measured. It weighs about 2 % of the body and uses about 20 watts, a small light bulb. The cerebellum alone holds about 80 % of the neurons in 10 % of the volume.
À la fin du XIXe siècle, Santiago Ramón: At the end of the 19th century Santiago Ramón y Cajal showed that the nervous system is made of distinct cells, neurons, using a stain invented by Camillo Golgi, who argued the opposite, a continuous network. They shared the 1906 Nobel Prize, in a tense atmosphere. And no, we do not use 10 % of our brain: imaging shows every region is used.
Gage (1848) : le lobe frontal et le cara: Gage (1848): the frontal lobe and character. Broca (1861): language. Plasticity: learning changes the brain (London taxis).
En 1848, une barre à mine traverse le cr: In 1848 an iron rod went through the skull of Phineas Gage, a railway worker. He survived and lived twelve more years, but his friends said "Gage was no longer Gage": the frontal lobe also governs character. In 1861 Paul Broca autopsied a patient, Leborgne, who could only say one syllable, "tan": a lesion in the left frontal lobe. That is Broca's area, linked to producing language.
Le cerveau, pourtant, se réorganise tout: Yet the brain reorganises itself throughout life: that is plasticity. After a stroke, other regions can take over a lost function. In 2000 Eleanor Maguire showed that London taxi drivers, who learn 25,000 streets, have a larger part of the hippocampus. Learning literally changes the brain.
Pas de cerveau gauche « logique » ni dro: No "logical" left brain or "creative" right brain (Nielsen, 2013). A coloured MRI image is not proof (the dead salmon).
Le « cerveau gauche logique » contre le: The "logical left brain" versus "creative right brain" is a myth. Some functions are more lateralised, like language, but the two hemispheres work together constantly. In 2013 a study of more than 1,000 brains by Jared Nielsen and colleagues found no overall "dominance" of one hemisphere in individuals.
L'imagerie elle-même demande de la prude: Imaging itself calls for caution. In 2009 a team "detected" activity in the brain of a dead salmon placed in a scanner, to show the danger of poorly corrected statistics; it received an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012. A pretty coloured image is not proof. And the brain feels no pain: some operations are done on an awake patient, who talks during the procedure.
Quatre stades (Piaget) ; conservation ac: Four stages (Piaget); conservation acquired around 7. Babies know things earlier than he thought (Baillargeon).
Jean Piaget a commencé en observant ses: Jean Piaget started by observing his own children, notebook in hand. He described four broad stages: sensorimotor, where the baby discovers the world through senses and movement; preoperational; concrete operations; formal operations, where one reasons about abstract ideas.
Vers 4 ans, l'enfant comprend qu'autrui: Around age 4, children understand that others can believe something false (Sally-Anne, 1985). Proximal zone: what you can do with help (Vygotsky).
Le test de Sally et Anne : Sally cache u: The Sally-Anne test: Sally hides a marble in a basket and leaves. Anne moves it to a box. Where will Sally look? Before about age 4, the child answers "in the box", where it really is. After that, the child understands that Sally believes something other than what is true. That is theory of mind, tested this way by Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith in 1985.
Lev Vygotski insiste, lui, sur le rôle d: Lev Vygotsky stressed the role of others: the zone of proximal development is what the child can do with help but not yet alone. Good teaching aims at that zone, neither too easy nor out of reach. This game tries to do the same with its levels.
Le réconfort compte plus que la nourritu: Comfort matters more than food (Harlow). A secure attachment allows exploration (Bowlby, Ainsworth).
Dans les années 1950, Harry Harlow élève: In the 1950s Harry Harlow raised baby monkeys with two artificial "mothers": one made of wire that gave milk, the other of soft cloth with no milk. The babies spent their time clinging to the cloth mother. Comfort matters more than food. These very cruel experiments also fed into animal ethics.
John Bowlby en tire la théorie de l'atta: John Bowlby drew from this the theory of attachment: a secure bond lets the child explore, knowing it can come back. Mary Ainsworth measured it with the "strange situation": a child, its mother, a stranger, and a door that closes. As for the "Mozart effect", it comes from a 1993 study on students, with a modest, short-lived gain that was poorly replicated afterwards: classical music does not make babies smarter.
Big Five (OCEAN) : des continuums, pas d: Big Five (OCEAN): continuums, not types. 40-60 % heritable, they change with age.
Ces traits sont héritables à environ 40: These traits are about 40 to 60 % heritable according to twin studies, and the rest comes mainly from each person's own experiences rather than the shared family. They also change: in adulthood we become on average more conscientious and more agreeable. And conscientiousness predicts school success almost as well as intelligence.
Les tests qui ne tiennent pas: Tests that do not hold up
The MBTI is unstable (Pittenger, 1993). Humours and phrenology: abandoned, only words remain.
Le MBTI classe les gens en 16 types. Il: The MBTI sorts people into 16 types. It sells very well, but many people change type when they retake the test a few weeks later, as David Pittenger pointed out in 1993. A type that changes with the day of the test does not measure much that is stable.
L'histoire est pleine de systèmes abando: History is full of abandoned systems. Hippocrates and Galen classified temperaments by four humours; we are left with the words sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, melancholic. Franz Joseph Gall's phrenology read character in the bumps of the skull; French is left with "having the maths bump". The scenery changes; the urge to be put in a box remains.
Lui, c'est un chauffard ; moi, j'étais p: He's a reckless driver; I was in a hurry
Erreur fondamentale d'attribution (Ross,: Fundamental attribution error (Ross, 1977): others "are" like that, we "were" in a situation. Introvert ≠ shy.
L'erreur fondamentale d'attribution cons: The fundamental attribution error is explaining other people's behaviour by their character, and our own by circumstances. Someone cuts you off: they are a reckless driver. You cut someone off: you were in a hurry. Lee Ross named it in 1977.
Être introverti, au sens psychologique,: Being introverted, in the psychological sense, does not mean being shy: it mainly means drawing energy from time alone rather than from interaction. An introvert can speak in public perfectly well; they just need to recharge afterwards. The words introvert and extravert come from Carl Jung, in 1921.
Stress aigu = mobilisation ; stress chro: Acute stress = mobilisation; chronic stress = wear (Selye, 1936). A little arousal helps, too much paralyses (Yerkes-Dodson).
En 1936, Hans Selye décrit dans une lett: In 1936 Hans Selye described in a letter to Nature rats subjected to all kinds of harm, which all reacted the same way; he later called this reaction stress. Acute stress mobilises: cortisol releases energy to cope. It is chronic stress that wears you down: cortisol kept high for a long time weakens immunity and memory.
La loi de Yerkes et Dodson, établie en 1: The Yerkes-Dodson law, established in 1908 on mice, draws a bell curve: a little arousal improves performance, too much paralyses it. A little stage fright helps. Against chronic stress, several meta-analyses put regular physical activity at a level close to psychotherapy for mild to moderate anxiety and depression.
Le loto ne rend pas heureux longtemps: The lottery does not make you happy for long
Adaptation hédonique : on revient vers s: Hedonic adaptation: we return towards our usual level (Brickman, 1978). Relationships best predict well-being (Harvard, since 1938).
Après un grand gain ou une grande perte,: After a big win or a big loss, we largely return to our usual level of happiness: that is hedonic adaptation. In 1978 Philip Brickman compared lottery winners and people who had become paraplegic: some time later, the gaps in happiness were far smaller than you would imagine. The return is not always complete, but it is powerful.
Qu'est-ce qui compte, alors ? L'étude de: So what matters? The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed men since 1938, then their families. Its conclusion, summed up by its current director, Robert Waldinger: good relationships make us happier and healthier. Social ties are the best predictor of a long and happy life.
7 à 9 heures de sommeil. Écriture expres: 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Expressive writing (Pennebaker, 1986), mindfulness: real but modest effects.
Le sommeil consolide la mémoire, et en m: Sleep consolidates memory, and missing it degrades mood and attention. For an adult, recommendations range from 7 to 9 hours a night; regularly getting under 6 hours is linked to many health risks.
Écrire sur ses émotions difficiles quelq: Writing about difficult emotions for a few days in a row can also help: James Pennebaker's expressive writing protocol in 1986 was followed by fewer doctor's visits, with real but modest effects. And mindfulness, brought into medicine by Jon Kabat-Zinn, offers eight weeks of secularised meditation exercises. Conversely, occupational exhaustion, burnout, described in 1974, was recognised by the WHO in 2019 as an occupational phenomenon.
Autre outil très ancien : le palais de m: Another very old tool: the memory palace, or method of loci, which goes back to Antiquity. You mentally place each item to remember in a familiar place, then walk the route again to find them. Legend ties it to the Greek poet Simonides of Ceos: the only survivor of a banquet whose roof had collapsed, he is said to have identified the victims by remembering where each had sat. Cicero tells it in 55 BCE, in On the Orator. Memory champions still use it. In a list, we remember the beginning and the end best: these are the primacy and recency effects. And goldfish retain associations for weeks.
La motivation intrinsèque, c'est agir po: Intrinsic motivation is acting for the activity itself; extrinsic, for a reward or to avoid punishment. A trap: rewarding an activity you already enjoy can reduce the desire to do it. That is the overjustification effect: the activity becomes a means to get the reward, and loses its appeal when the reward stops. Edward Deci measured it as early as 1971: students paid to solve a puzzle spent markedly less free time on it once the payment stopped.
On repousse surtout ce qui ennuie, angoi: We mainly put off what bores us, worries us or seems vague. Procrastination is first an escape from an unpleasant emotion, not a lack of willpower. Once started, a task stays "open" in the mind: that is the Zeigarnik effect. The Soviet psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik described it in 1927. The idea came from her professor Kurt Lewin: a waiter remembered unpaid orders in detail, and forgot them once the bill was settled. Hence simple advice: start for five minutes, just to open the task.
Ses expériences de conservation sont cél: His conservation experiments are famous: pour water from a wide glass into a tall narrow one, and a five-year-old often thinks there is more, judging by the height. Around 7, the child understands that pouring does not change the amount. But the stages are less rigid than Piaget thought: Renée Baillargeon's experiments suggest babies grasp earlier that a hidden object still exists. In 1985, with Elizabeth Spelke and Stanley Wasserman, she showed that 5-month-old babies look longer at a screen that seems to pass through a hidden box, whereas Piaget placed object permanence around 9 months.
Le modèle des Big Five décrit la personn: The Big Five model describes personality through five broad traits: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, OCEAN in English. These five factors first emerged from a study of US Air Force officers by Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal in 1958, published in 1961; the name Big Five was coined by Lewis Goldberg in 1981. It is the best-validated model in psychology. Each trait is a continuum: you are not introverted or extraverted, you are more or less extraverted.
